title: The Throne verse
hookLine: the Living, the Sustainer, whose Throne extends over heavens and earth, who never tires of guarding them (2:255)

cards: Count what you're guarding right now. Your phone's battery. A child's fever, or a parent's appointments.
The inbox. The rent. The plant on the windowsill you keep forgetting.
Guarding a dozen things at once can leave you tired by evening, sometimes too tired to sleep. Last year you heard the story of Ayat al-Kursi and the names inside it.
This year, read it where al-Baqarah places it, line by line, to its last picture: guarding without tiring. Today: the Throne verse.

teach.h: NO TRADE, NO FRIEND, NO INTERCESSOR
teach.b: Start with the verse just before it. Verse two hundred fifty-four warns of a day with no trading, no friendship and no intercession: every human safety net, gone.
Verse two hundred fifty-five answers with who holds everything when those are gone.

In Pickthall's words: “Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.” Then it widens, step by step. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him.
Who could intercede with Him, except by His permission? So the intercession verse two fifty-four took away comes back, but only through Him.
He knows what's before people and behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.
Then the picture that names the verse: “His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them.”

teach.h: LA YA'UDUHU: IT DOESN'T WEIGH ON HIM
teach.b: The Arabic for never weary is la ya'uduhu: it doesn't weigh on Him, doesn't bend Him under the load, a word used for a branch sagging under weight. The whole sky and earth don't make Him sag.
And the last line: “He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.” Many Muslims recite this verse after each obligatory prayer and before sleep.
The bedtime habit fits: you lie down still guarding the phone, the child, the rent, and the verse hands the watch to someone who doesn't sleep and doesn't tire.

how: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi after each obligatory prayer, before sleep, and when leaving home, and children often learn it early as a verse of protection.

games.q: you're lying awake, still guarding everything: the phone, the child, the rent. what do many Muslims do at this moment?
games.why: recite it: the verse hands the watch to the one who neither sleeps nor tires.

practice: If you know the verse in Arabic, say it slowly, pausing after each sentence to recall what it means.

If not, take it in English, one line per breath: the Alive, the Eternal; no slumber, no sleep; everything belongs to Him; no one intercedes but by His leave; He knows before and behind; His throne includes heavens and earth; guarding them doesn't tire Him; the Sublime, the Tremendous.

wordCard.voice: Ayat al-Kursi. The Throne Verse, al-Baqarah 2:255: the Alive who never sleeps, whose throne includes the heavens and earth, and who never tires of guarding them.

orig.note: Arabic: and guarding them does not weary Him, the last picture of 2:255.

carryVoice: Your line: he never tires. The verse keeps the watch through the night. Rest easy.
